topicA.name: AI Visibility and Search Optimization for B2B

resources.headline: 4 Datasets On AI Visibility: ChatGPT Sends 0.62% Of Google’s Organic Traffic via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
resources.fullText: If an AI visibility dashboard helped you win budget this year, read four datasets before your next quarterly review. Together, they show AI assistants send a sliver of the traffic Google sends. They also show that none of these datasets could isolate the hidden AI influence many of us assumed was turning up in Direct and branded search. That doesn’t make AI visibility a sham. It means most of the ways we measure it wouldn’t pass a basic data quality test. One Event, Or The Start Of A Trend? On Oct. 22, 2026, Rand Fishkin published a 5-Minute Whiteboard on the SparkToro Blog titled “Is AI Visibility a Marketing Boondoggle?” The next day, Amanda Natividad, SparkToro’s chief evangelist, sent her Audience Research Newsletter asking, “What if AI visibility is a sham?” A long time ago, I learned to separate events from trends. Two warnings from co-authors of the same book, Zero Click Marketing, who work at the same company and publish a day apart, look more like one event than two. But the data underneath their warnings came from other people. And it has been piling up. Source Published Sample What it found Kevin Indig, Growth Memo Oct. 19, 2026 12 GA4 properties, plus 632 correlation tests on four brands No reliable link between AI visibility and later direct traffic or branded search Marie Haynes Oct. 21, 2026 100 sites, 145 million+ sessions, 12 months ChatGPT sent 0.62% of Google organic’s volume; all LLMs, 0.73% SEO Works Data Sept. 2025 to Aug. 2026 95 GA4 properties Organic sent 39x more traffic than AI assistants Ahrefs May 26, 2025 75,000 brands Branded search volume correlated only 0.392 with AI Overview brand visibility The Traffic Numbers Are Small, And The Conversion Story Is Mixed Marie Haynes looked at 12 months of GA4 data across 100 websites. ChatGPT visitors converted at 13.8%, against 3.02% for Google organic. That’s more than 4.5 times better, and it’s the stat AI visibility vendors will quote. But here’s the stat they won’t. Google still drove 96.5% of total conversions in her dataset, and Google organic drove 27 times more conversions than all LLMs combined. She also found that the exponential growth in ChatGPT sessions ended in August 2025, around the release of GPT-5. SEO Works found a narrower edge. AI referrals converted at 7.18% versus 6.08% for organic, a pooled ratio of 1.18. Yet AI traffic converted worse on 23 of the 63 sites with enough volume to compare. For B2B product businesses, AI converted at 0.62 times the organic rate. The line from that study I’d tape to every SEO manager’s monitor is this one. A 5% lift in organic search delivered 10.3 additional conversions per site per month. Doubling AI referral traffic delivered 6.6. The Hidden Influence Hasn’t Shown Up Yet The usual rebuttal is that clicks were never the point. People see a brand in a ChatGPT answer, don’t click, and then search for it or type in the URL later. Kevin Indig went looking for that. At first, eight of his 12 properties showed Direct traffic growing from August to September. Then he filtered for engaged sessions. Across the filtered January-September sample, total Direct rose 140.9%, while engaged Direct changed by −1.0%. On one site, GA4 recorded 409,000 Direct sessions, and only 198 were engaged. That’s bots, not buyers. He then ran 632 tests on four brands, comparing weekly AI visibility with Direct traffic and branded search at delays of zero to six weeks. When he shifted the data to deliberately wrong dates as a placebo check, several of those mismatched alignments correlated as strongly as the real ones. His conclusion: “An effect could still exist. I just couldn’t isolate it.” Natividad tied this back to an Ahrefs study of 75,000 brands from May 2025. Branded web mentions correlated at 0.664 with AI Overview brand visibility, and branded anchors at 0.527. Branded search volume came in last at 0.392. If AI visibility reliably produced branded search, she argued, that number should be much higher. See also: Direct Traffic & Popularity – Correlation, Not Causation What Fishkin And Natividad Actually Concluded Neither of them said AI doesn’t matter. Fishkin wrote that AI is “probably quite influential on some buyers in some sectors.” He credited Mike King with the better frame, that AI is “more like a brand channel, a digital billboard if you will, and it should be invested-in and measured as such.” Natividad put it more sharply. “Familiarity itself is a marketing outcome.” Then she added the sentence that matters most for anyone building a dashboard. “If we can’t prove it, we shouldn’t trust the attribution just because it seems right.” The Measurement Industry Saw This Coming In May The SEO world is arriving late to a conversation the PR measurement world started months ago. On May 20, 2026, AMEC, the International Association for the Measurement and Evaluation of Communication, launched its GEO Principles at its Global Summit in Dublin. Two days later, I admitted that I’d been treating AI citations as the new search rankings and that framing was wrong. Appearing in an AI answer is an output, whether it changes what people understand, believe, or do is an outcome. AMEC has also gone a layer deeper with a companion white paper, “AMEC Data Quality Principles: Tackling the Unstructured Data Quality Challenges in the AI Era.” Its lead author is Rob Key, founder and CEO of Converseon, and it was produced with the Global Data Quality Initiative, a coalition that includes the Insights Association, ESOMAR, and the Market Research Society. The paper was written for social listening and media analysts, not SEOs. Read it with an AI visibility dashboard open in another tab anyway. It proposes four questions any data set should pass before anyone acts on it. AMEC Question What it asks How AI visibility data fails it Source Is the data from the sources we expect, and only those? Bot sessions inflating Direct, as in Indig’s 409,000-session example Accuracy Is the metadata complete and faithful t
keyNotes: Surprisingly little traffic comes from AI: Even with all the buzz around AI tools like ChatGPT, they send a tiny fraction of website visitors compared to regular Google searches. For example, ChatGPT only sent 0.62% of the traffic Google organic search did in one study.

AI visitors might be high quality, but low quantity: While people who come from AI tools might be more likely to buy something (one study showed they converted 4.5 times better), Google still drives 27 times more total sales because it sends so many more people to websites.

It's hard to prove AI's "hidden" influence: The idea that people see a brand in an AI answer and then search for it later is difficult to track. One expert found no clear link, and many direct visits to websites were actually from automated programs (bots), not real customers.

Many ways of measuring AI impact are flawed: It's easy for data to be misleading, like counting automated programs (bots) as real visitors. This means that many reports on AI's impact might not be accurate unless the data quality is carefully checked.

Think of AI as a brand builder, not a direct sales tool: Experts suggest that appearing in an AI answer is more like a "digital billboard" that builds familiarity with a brand, which is valuable, even if it doesn't immediately lead to a click or sale.
resources.question: The article suggests that AI mentions are more like a "digital billboard" for building brand familiarity, rather than directly driving clicks. In your own work, where do you encounter situations where something is clearly valuable, but its direct impact is incredibly difficult to measure or attribute?

resources.headline: Scrunch vs. Ahrefs: AI visibility tracking comparison
resources.fullText: If you’re weighing Scrunch vs Ahrefs, you’re probably asking a bigger question underneath it: do I buy a specialist tool for AI search, or let the SEO platform I already use handle it? People are asking AI tools for recommendations before they ever hit a website, and when Google shows an AI summary, searchers end their browsing session more often, according to Pew Research Center. So it makes sense that you want to see how your brand shows up in those answers. Here’s the quick version. Scrunch is built for AEO. It tracks your AI visibility and also changes what AI bots see when they crawl your site. Ahrefs Brand Radar adds AI brand monitoring and citation tracking to the keyword, backlink, and site audit tools you may already use. If you’re starting a dedicated AEO program, Scrunch is worth a close look. If your team lives in Ahrefs, Brand Radar will feel like home. Either way, AEO works alongside AI SEO and traditional SEO, so you don’t have to pick one world over the other. We’ll compare the two on engine and surface coverage, prompt methodology, citation and reporting detail, actionability, integrations, pricing, and best-fit team. One more thing: HubSpot sells its own AEO products, and will show up after the neutral comparison, judged on the same criteria. Table of Contents Scrunch vs. Ahrefs at a Glance Scrunch vs. Ahrefs Engine Coverage and Surfaces Scrunch vs. Ahrefs Reporting Depth and Methodology Scrunch vs. Ahrefs Actionability and Workflows Scrunch vs. Ahrefs Pricing and Scalability Who Should Choose Scrunch or Ahrefs The HubSpot-Native Path For AEO Measurement Alternatives Worth a Look Decision Matrix and Next Steps Frequently Asked Questions About Scrunch vs. Ahrefs Scrunch vs. Ahrefs at a Glance Choose Scrunch if you want active website optimization for AI crawlers, product-level shopping visibility, or agency pitch workspaces. Choose Ahrefs Brand Radar if you want AI tracking inside an all-in-one SEO platform, backed by a large database of real user search prompts and multi-channel tracking across YouTube, Reddit, and TikTok. Scrunch is an Agent Experience Platform (AXP) from Sitecore. It detects AI agents such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity at the edge and serves them a token-light, structured version of your pages, while human visitors see the normal site. Ahrefs Brand Radar tracks AI visibility from inside the Ahrefs ecosystem, so the AI data sits next to Site Explorer, Keywords Explorer, and Rank Tracker. A surface is a place where answers or brand mentions appear, such as a Google AI Overview, Google AI Mode, a YouTube video, or a Reddit thread. Comparing the two tools gets easier once you keep those terms separate. Ahrefs Brand Radar covers 7 platforms on every tier. Scrunch covers 4 LLMs on Core and 9 on Enterprise, with Claude, Gemini, Meta AI, Google AI Mode, and Grok added at the higher tier. If you need broad engine coverage without an enterprise contract, Brand Radar has the edge. Scrunch’s depth shows up elsewhere, in its Shopping module and its bot-side tools. Ahrefs goes wider on surfaces that aren’t LLMs, tracking YouTube transcripts and titles, Reddit, TikTok in beta, and a GBP Monitor for Google Business Profiles. Which engines matter most for my category? Start with the engines your buyers use, then work outward. Your analytics referrals, sales call notes, and customer surveys will show where buyers say they research. Google deserves early attention because of its reach. Research found that 18% of Google searches in March 2025 produced an AI summary, and the rate climbed with longer, question-style searches. If your buyers research with long, conversational queries, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode belong in your first tracking set. Our guide to the top search engines can help you map where your audience searches, and the evolution of search gives context on why that mix keeps shifting. Ecommerce teams should weigh Scrunch’s product-level shopping visibility. Brands with strong video or community footprints should weigh Ahrefs’ YouTube and Reddit tracking. How should I validate coverage during a trial? Scrunch offers a 7-day free trial on entry tiers. Ahrefs doesn’t offer free trials or discounts on Brand Radar, so ask your rep what a pilot looks like. keyNotes: People are now asking AI tools for recommendations *before* they even visit a website, and when Google shows an AI summary (a quick answer generated by AI), people often stop browsing completely, according to Pew Research Center. This means it's super important for businesses to know how their brand shows up in these AI answers.

One tool, Scrunch, is designed to not only track how your brand appears in AI answers but also to actively change what AI "bots" (the computer programs that power AI) see when they look at your website. It can even show a special, simplified version of your site just for these bots, while human visitors see the regular site.

The other tool, Ahrefs Brand Radar, helps you monitor how your brand is mentioned by AI, but it's built to fit right into other tools you might already use for traditional search engine optimization (SEO), which is about making your website show up higher in search results. It also tracks where your brand is mentioned across places like YouTube, Reddit, and TikTok.

Google is becoming a big player in AI answers; research found that 18% of Google searches in March 2025 resulted in an AI summary, especially for longer, question-style searches. This means if your customers ask detailed questions, your brand needs to be visible in these AI overviews.
resources.question: The article mentions that businesses should figure out which AI 'engines' (like ChatGPT, which generates AI answers) and 'surfaces' (like Google AI Overviews or YouTube, where those answers appear) their customers use for research. Thinking about your own work or business, how do you currently discover where your audience looks for information or recommendations, and how might the growing use of AI change where you need to focus your attention to be seen?

resources.headline: Obstacles in marketing automation and how to fix them [2026]
resources.fullText: Most obstacles in marketing automation aren’t actually automation problems. 86.4% of marketing teams now use AI somewhere in their workflows. Yet, measuring ROI still tops the challenge list at 33%, according to HubSpot’s 2026 State of Marketing Report. Ultimately, marketing automation issues are rarely tool problems. They are most often caused by unclear strategy, bad data, siloed tools, and weak team alignment. The automation platform executes those problems faster and at greater scale. This guide diagnoses the seven most common marketing automation challenges, what breaks, and the specific fixes. Use it to identify and repair underperforming automation workflows. Table of Contents Why Obstacles in Marketing Automation Start With Strategy Obstacles in marketing automation come from bad data. Problems With Marketing Automation When Sales and Marketing Are Misaligned Problems With Marketing Automation Caused by Siloed Tools When Automation Hurts Customer Experience Preventing Compliance Issues in Automated Journeys Measuring and Improving Automation Performance Frequently Asked Questions About Marketing Automation Problems The fix is a system. Why Obstacles in Marketing Automation Start With Strategy Most obstacles in marketing automation trace back to a missing or unclear go-to-market strategy. Teams that automate without defined goals and lifecycle journey logic end up with more signals, like emails, branches, and alerts. But, that doesn’t result in more sales pipeline. The symptoms are easy to spot once someone names them: Every contact receives the same nurture track regardless of lifecycle stage or ICP fit. Workflows accumulate for years because nobody documented why they exist or whether they should stay on. Campaign volume rises while conversion rates stay flat. These obstacles in marketing automation are strategy failures. They sit behind many of the classic marketing automation mistakes teams repeat every year. Part of the confusion is that automation itself has changed. Modern workflow automation is no longer a backend ops function. Instead, AI-augmented workflows have turned it into a frontline growth lever that reads context (buyer behavior, persona, funnel stage) and adjusts the next best action. A tool with that much reach deserves a real strategy behind it. So the fix? Always start with strategy. Before building any automation, the team should first define the following. The Why (Goals): Every automation exists to move a business metric, whether that’s a revenue goal, an efficiency goal, or an engagement goal. This is also where the team should debate what to automate versus what deliberately not to automate. The Who (Clear, Aligned Segmentation): A highly personalized experience is why 93.2% of marketers say personalized, segmented experiences drive more leads and purchases (2026 State of Marketing). The How (Entry, Exit, and Suppression Criteria): Who enters, what removes them, and which audiences must never be enrolled? Most “automation gone rogue” incidents are missing exit criteria. The Owner: A named human should be accountable for each automation’s performance and ongoing maintenance. As the strategy evolves, so should automation. In 2026, marketing automation strategy also means deciding what AI is allowed to do versus where a human stays in the loop. Traditional rule-based workflows execute predefined steps. Now, AI agents can independently research, draft, and decide what to do. Teams need an explicit policy for which decisions stay human before they scale automation. AI Agents Builder Build custom agents and workflows on one canvas, powered by the CRM data you already have. Make your dream workflows Control which actions run on their own Run it once or repeat it across your team Follow your playbook – not a generic one Get Started Learn more Get Started Download FreeAll fields are required. Form not available You're all set! Click this link to access this resource at any time. Download Now Obstacles in marketing automation come from bad data. Remember: an automation platform is only as good as the CRM records underneath it. Duplicate contacts could trigger duplicate sequences. Stale job titles tend to route leads to the wrong owner. Missing lifecycle properties enroll customers in prospect nurtures. Every one of these is a high-stakes mistake no marketer wants attached to their funnel. Bad data causes poor segmentation, broken personalization, and incorrect lead routing. The scope of the problem is bigger than most teams admit: Only 65% of marketers say they have high-quality data about their target audience, per HubSpot’s 2026 State of Marketing report. This number hasn’t improved year over year even as AI adoption soared. Part of the issue is that “clean” is no longer enough in today’s marketing landscape. The database also has to be complete in the dimensions modern AI-ready automation actually uses. A revenue-ready B2B database spans five signal types: Demographic data, like contacts and job titles. Firmographic data, like company size, industry, and geography. Technographic data, or the tools and account runs. Event-triggered data, like executive hires, funding, and acquisitions. And intent data. The trap most marketing teams fall into in today’s marketing is collection without consolidation. Sales teams still struggle to interpret the signals because they arrive fragmented across tools instead of consolidated on one record. This also adds natural data decay (people change jobs, companies get acquired, etc.) that breaks the automation. AI simply raises the stakes further. Personalization models, scoring agents, and routing logic all consume CRM data as ground truth. Bad inputs produce thousands of automated mistakes once agents start taking actions. A unified CRM, like HubSpot’s Smart CRM, is built for exactly this role: it gives marketing, sales, and customer success one shared record to automate against. keyNotes: Even though most marketing teams (86.4%) now use artificial intelligence (AI) in their work, their biggest challenge, for 33% of them, is proving if their automated efforts actually lead to more money.

When automated marketing tools don't work well, it's rarely the tool's fault; the real problems are usually a missing plan, bad customer information, different tools not sharing data, or teams not working together effectively.

A major reason automated marketing fails is a lack of clear strategy, meaning businesses often send more messages but don't get more sales because they haven't defined their goals or who they're trying to reach.

Automated marketing is only as effective as the customer information it uses; bad or incomplete data will cause the automation to make mistakes, like sending the wrong message, but much faster and at a larger scale.
resources.question: The article emphasizes that a clear strategy, including deciding what AI should do versus what a human should handle, is crucial for successful automation. In your own work, where do you see opportunities to automate tasks, and more importantly, what critical decisions or interactions do you believe should *always* remain in human hands, and why?

resources.headline: Digital marketing strategy for B2B business: the parts, and why they have to work together
resources.fullText: An expert analysis on building a cohesive B2B digital marketing strategy, highlighting the importance of integrated components for long-term success.
keyNotes: For businesses that sell to other businesses (what we call B2B), having a well-thought-out plan for how they do their online marketing is essential.
The article highlights that for this online marketing plan to truly work, all its different pieces, or "components," must be connected and work together.
This idea of making sure everything is connected and working as one unit is called building a "cohesive" strategy, and it's presented as a key to success.
Ultimately, the main goal of having all these online marketing parts work together is to help the business achieve success that lasts for a long time.
resources.question: The article emphasizes that for a business's online marketing to succeed long-term, all its parts must work together. In your own work, what are the different 'parts' or tasks you handle, and how well do they currently connect and support each other to achieve your long-term goals?

resources.headline: Most B2B content misses. Here's how to make it convert.
resources.fullText: A strategy deep-dive on making B2B content convert by mapping it to real buyer pain points and aligning cross-functional teams.
keyNotes: The main goal of information created for businesses (called "B2B content") is to make it "convert," meaning it should actually lead to new customers or sales.
A key way to make this content work is by understanding and directly addressing the specific problems or challenges that potential business customers are experiencing.
For content to be truly effective, it's important for different departments within a company, like sales and marketing, to work together towards a shared goal.
The article suggests that a thorough and well-planned approach, or "strategy deep-dive," is necessary to achieve successful content that turns into business results.
resources.question: The article highlights that understanding customer problems and getting different company teams to work together are crucial for success. In your own work, how might you better discover the real challenges your customers face, and what steps could you take to ensure everyone in your organization is united in addressing them?

resources.headline: AI Is Accelerating Insights — Can Your Business Keep Up?
resources.fullText: < Featured Blogs Home > Featured Blogs > AI Is Accelerating Insights — Can Your Business Keep Up? AI Is Accelerating Insights — Can Your Business Keep Up? Companies are racing to put AI into marketing and go-to-market (GTM) processes, expecting faster analysis, richer customer intelligence, greater productivity, and ultimately better decisions. Yet there is a challenge hiding inside those ambitions: AI can accelerate the flow of insights much faster than an organization can accelerate its ability to act on them. That matters, because insights have a shelf life: A shift in buyer behavior, an emerging customer need, a change in campaign performance, or a competitive signal becomes less valuable when it takes weeks to travel through the organization and influence a decision. Many businesses already have an insights-to-impact gap. Forrester data shows that among B2B data and analytics decision-makers, 33% cite a lack of trust in data sources as a barrier to acting on insights; 29% cite a lack of trust in analysis; and 28% point to a lack of skills to interpret insights. My new report, Close The Gap Between Insights And Impact, also highlights the growing importance of data literacy, AI fluency, and the ability to interpret insights. AI puts additional pressure on all of these. It can give organizations more signals, more analysis, and more recommendations at greater speed. For a business that already struggles to turn insights into action, AI could widen the gap rather than close it. Consider what this means for a GTM organization: AI detects a shift in buyer behavior, and marketing sees the signal first; sales continues with the existing conversation, customer success has additional evidence from existing customers, and product teams have relevant usage data. Everyone holds a piece of the picture, yet nobody changes course quickly enough. The business had the insight and still missed the opportunity. Our research highlights the importance of sharing customer, market, and performance knowledge across marketing, sales, product, and customer success to improve decisions and coordinated execution. As AI increases the flow of information, that ability becomes even more consequential. GTM leaders need to help their organizations turn AI insights into action by identifying which signals matter, challenging existing assumptions, making decisions, coordinating action, and determining whether the action produced the intended customer and business outcome. Turn AI Insights Into Action Faster This brings a different question into the AI conversation. Companies understandably ask where to deploy AI and which use cases can create value. Marketing and GTM leaders should add another question: How much faster can our business turn a new signal into a better customer or commercial decision? The answer depends on what happens across the entire loop, from signal to interpretation, decision, action, outcome, and adaptation. The loop cannot stop with execution. Teams need to understand whether a changed message improves engagement, whether a different sales approach advances an opportunity, or whether an experiment changes customer behavior. Those outcomes become evidence for the next decision. The faster an organization can move through this cycle while preserving sound judgment, the greater its ability to respond while the relevant insights still matter. Earlier Forrester research explored practices that help businesses continuously learn and adapt. The new report extends that thinking by connecting customer, market, and performance insights more directly with decisions, actions, and measurable business impact. This may become one of the less obvious dividing lines in the AI race. Access to AI will spread rapidly; so will the ability to generate and analyze enormous amounts of information. Sustainable advantage will increasingly depend on what happens next: whether businesses can understand what matters, mobilize the right parts of the GTM organization, learn from the outcome, and continuously improve the next decision. AI is compressing the time between signal and opportunity — businesses need to compress the time between uncovering insights and deriving impact from them. Read Close The Gap Between Insights And Impact to explore how organizations can turn customer, market, and performance insights into action and measurable business outcomes. If you’re considering what this means for your own marketing or GTM organization, reach out or book a session with me. We can explore where insights get stuck today and what it would take to turn them into customer and business impact faster.
